sections.description: This section introduces the patient's demographic background, presenting symptoms, and the initial clinical evaluation upon presentation to the emergency department and subsequent transfer to the obstetrical-gynecological division. It covers the key elements of the history, physical examination, initial laboratory findings, and early symptomatic management that set the stage for the diagnostic workup.
subtopics: Patient demographics and obstetric history: nulliparous woman in her 40s, G1P0A1, BMI 33, second trimester pregnancy (21 weeks GA)
Chief complaints: severe acute abdominal pain in the upper left quadrant and pelvis (VAS=5), associated with mild dyspnea
Prenatal screening history: low-risk aneuploidy screening, normal fetal morphology, negative NIPT
Emergency department evaluation: vital signs (oxygen saturation 97%, heart rate 74 bpm, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg), normal ECG
Abdominal examination findings: abdominal enlargement exceeding gestational age, tender swelling, taut-elastic mass (18 cm) in the upper left quadrant, no ascites
Bimanual vaginal examination: fixed, rounded, hard mass (~9 cm) in the lesser pelvis bulging at the posterior fornix
Initial laboratory findings: iron deficiency anemia (Hb 9.9 g/L, ferritin 25 mcg/L), elevated CRP (1.39 mg/dL), leukocytosis with neutrophilia consistent with pregnancy-related changes
Hospital course complications: low-grade fever, negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR, Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary tract infection
Initial symptomatic management: paracetamol analgesia and semi-orthostatic positioning, reduction of pain from VAS 5 to 1

sections.section_title: Imaging Evaluation and Tumor Marker Assessment
sections.description: This section details the diagnostic imaging modalities employed and the tumor marker evaluation that informed the differential diagnosis. It explains the rationale for using ultrasound and non-contrast MRI in pregnancy, the specific imaging characteristics of the two masses, and the interpretation of CA-125 and other tumor markers in the context of pregnancy.
subtopics: Ultrasound findings: two large unilocular cystic masses with regular margins and peripheral vascularization; upper mass 18×12×7 cm from left subphrenic region to uterine fundus; lower mass 9.5×8×8 cm adherent to posterior intramural-subserosal myoma with cystic degeneration (58×71 mm)
Rationale and safety considerations for non-contrast MRI in pregnancy: avoiding gadolinium due to fetal risks; 1.5-T MRI safety after first trimester

MRI findings: thick walls (1.4 cm), T1 and T2 fat-sat inhomogeneous fluid content, focal hyperintense solid components, unclear cleavage of caudal mass with continuity to posterior leiomyoma, no adenopathy
Tumor marker panel: normal CA 19-9, CA 15-3, CEA, β2-microglobulin, and LDH; elevated CA-125 (41.8 U/mL, normal <35 U/mL) with increasing trend from 36 U/mL two weeks prior
Physiological variations of CA-125 during pregnancy: first trimester peak (median 23 U/mL), third trimester peak (median 21 U/mL), second trimester nadir (median 14 U/mL)
Interpretation challenges: elevated CA-125 in benign conditions (endometriosis, adenomyosis, pregnancy, myoma) versus ovarian cancer screening utility
Limitations of imaging in pregnancy: 'steric bulk' of gravid uterus obscuring connective stalks and feeding vessels, preventing definitive identification of mass origin

sections.description: This section explores the diagnostic reasoning process, weighing the imaging and laboratory findings to construct a differential diagnosis. It explains why the masses were initially interpreted as decidualized endometriomas, how the caudal mass was attributed to a degenerating leiomyoma, and the multidisciplinary rationale for proceeding to surgery despite the lack of definitive guidelines for pelvic masses in pregnancy.
subtopics: Differential diagnosis framework for abdominal masses in pregnancy: prevalence of leiomyomas (0.3–10.1%) versus adnexal masses (1–6%)
Imaging-based differential: decidualized endometriomas (cystic appearance, CA-125 elevation) versus cystic degenerating leiomyomas (continuity with uterine tissue)
Diagnostic ambiguity for the upper mass: inability to identify a stalk or feeding vessel, leading to assumption of ovarian origin (endometrioma)
Diagnostic reasoning for the caudal mass: continuity with posterior uterine wall suggesting myomatous origin with cystic degeneration
Attribution of dyspnea to mechanical compression from massive abdominal lesions without cardiopulmonary dysfunction
Multidisciplinary team composition and decision-making: surgeons, gynecologists, obstetricians, radiologists

Risk factors favoring surgical intervention: worsening clinical symptoms (pain, dyspnea), risk of complications (rupture, torsion, infection), potential for mass growth with fetal development, slight CA-125 elevation, and space limitations for uterine enlargement
Lack of definitive management guidelines for atypical pelvic masses in pregnancy and the role of individualized risk assessment

sections.description: This section covers the surgical procedure, including the decision to perform a laparotomy, the intraoperative discovery that both masses were uterine leiomyomas rather than ovarian cysts, the surgical technique employed, perioperative tocolytic and antibiotic management, and the pathological examination results that confirmed the diagnosis.
subtopics: Timing and indications for surgery: 21 weeks + 6 days, worsening symptoms, risk of complications, need for conclusive diagnosis
Surgical approach selection: longitudinal xifo-pubic laparotomy chosen over laparoscopy due to large mass size, multiple masses, intramural location, and advanced gestational age
Intraoperative steps: collection of peritoneal fluid for culture and cytology, abdominal exploration, verification of fetal cardiac activity
Surprise intraoperative finding: cranial mass was a huge pedunculated, atypical cystic leiomyoma (not an endometrioma), initially twisted and leaking, explaining the patient's fever
Surgical technique for upper myomectomy: gentle excision using double clamp, stalk transection, closure of exposed root with absorbable suture
Decision to leave caudal mass in situ: originating from uterine torus, fixed intramural-subserosal location, minimizing obstetric risk
Intraoperative fetal monitoring: serial transvaginal ultrasound for fetal viability throughout the procedure
Perioperative tocolysis: intraoperative progesterone 100 mg IM, continued daily until discharge, followed by hydroxyprogesterone caproate 341 mg IM every 3 days until delivery
Antibiotic management: intraoperative cefazolin 2 g IV, postoperative cefazolin 1 g IV three times daily plus clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily based on Klebsiella pneumoniae antibiogram
Pathology results: benign uterine leiomyomas with areas of ischemic necrosis near the twisted pedicle; negative peritoneal fluid cytology and cultures

sections.section_title: Postoperative Course, Pregnancy Follow-up, and Delivery Planning
sections.description: This section describes the postoperative management including treatment of surgical anemia, the obstetric follow-up plan, the decision-making process for mode of delivery, and the maternal and neonatal outcomes. It also covers the postpartum course and the natural regression of the residual myoma.
subtopics: Postoperative anemia management: Hb drop to 7.5 g/L, treatment with intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose 1 g) and two blood transfusions, achieving Hb 10.0 g/L
Hospital discharge: uncomplicated course, discharge 10 days post-surgery
Obstetric follow-up protocol: ultrasound every 3 weeks monitoring fetal growth (86th percentile per WHO chart) and amniotic fluid index
Delivery planning considerations: residual caudal myoma as potential obstacle to fetal head descent during vaginal delivery
Elective cesarean delivery at 37 weeks: rationale, use of previous surgical scar, risk minimization for uterine scar rupture
Maternal and neonatal outcomes: excellent neonatal outcome, successful breastfeeding
Postpartum course: partial regression of residual pelvic myoma to 7.5 cm, asymptomatic patient, patient preference to defer further surgery
Natural history of leiomyomas in puerperium: significant size decrease (mean 44.25%) by 6 weeks postpartum

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of Leiomyomas in Pregnancy and Clinical Lessons
sections.description: This section synthesizes the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying leiomyoma behavior during pregnancy, the reasons for diagnostic challenges, and the evidence-based clinical lessons drawn from this case and the literature. It covers the growth patterns of myomas across trimesters, mechanisms of cystic degeneration and torsion, and the principles guiding management of atypical masses in pregnancy.
subtopics: Leiomyoma growth patterns during pregnancy: 6.12% weekly increase between first and second trimesters, 3.10% between second and third, non-linear growth trend
Pathophysiology of cystic degeneration in pregnancy: rapid growth outstripping blood supply leading to ischemia, necrosis, and cystic change
Mechanisms of torsion in pedunculated leiomyomas and associated complications: ischemia, necrosis, fever, leakage
Why leiomyomas mimic adnexal masses: large size obscuring uterine origin, cystic degeneration resembling endometriomas, gravid uterus preventing identification of stalks
Decidualized endometriomas versus cystic leiomyomas: overlapping imaging features and the role of MRI in differentiation
Evidence on myomectomy during pregnancy: indications (torsion, persistent symptoms), risks (bleeding, pregnancy loss, preterm labor, uterine rupture), and laparotomy versus laparoscopy selection bias
Evidence on cesarean myomectomy: comparable hemodynamic outcomes to cesarean alone but longer hospitalization and surgery duration; correlation between myoma size and delivery week
Principles of comprehensive evaluation: bimanual examination, ultrasound with color Doppler, non-contrast MRI, serial CA-125 trends

Key clinical lessons: surgical management only for oncological suspicion or clinical complications, pregnancy preservation as priority, avoidance of overtreatment, delivery mode dependent on mass size, number, and anatomical location
